content: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a genetic disorder caused by a homozygous deletion of the SMN1 gene on chromosome 5, or a heterozygous deletion combined with a point mutation in the second SMN1 allele. This genetic defect leads to the degeneration of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord, resulting in progressive muscle weakness. Children with SMA type II are unable to walk independently and have a reduced life expectancy, while those with SMA type III can walk and generally have a normal life expectancy. The objective of this review was to determine whether drug treatments can slow or halt the progression of SMA types II and III and to assess the safety of these therapies. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized trials involving participants with confirmed genetic diagnoses of SMA types II or III. The primary outcome was the change in disability scores within one year of treatment initiation. Secondary outcomes included changes in muscle strength, ability to stand or walk, quality of life, time to death or full-time ventilation, and adverse events related to treatment. The review included 10 randomized, placebo-controlled trials with a total of 717 participants. These trials investigated various drugs, including creatine, gabapentin, hydroxyurea, nusinersen, olesoxime, phenylbutyrate, somatotropin, thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), valproic acid, and a combination of valproic acid with acetyl-L-carnitine (ALC). Treatment durations ranged from three to 24 months. None of the studies investigated the same treatment, and all had some degree of bias, though blinding, sequence generation, and reporting of primary outcomes were generally adequate. Moderate-certainty evidence showed that intrathecal nusinersen significantly improved motor function in children with SMA type II. Specifically, children treated with nusinersen experienced a 3.7-point improvement on the Hammersmith Functional Motor Scale Expanded (HFMSE), while those in the sham procedure group showed a 1.9-point decline (P < 0.01; n = 126). Higher scores on motor function scales indicate better function. In contrast, moderateand low-certainty evidence suggested that other interventions had no clinically meaningful effect on motor function in SMA types II or III. For example: Creatine showed a median change of 1 point higher on the Gross Motor Function Measure (GMFM) scale (95% CI: -1 to 2; n = 40). Combination therapy with valproic acid and ALC resulted in a mean difference (MD) of 0.64 on the Modified Hammersmith Functional Motor Scale (MHFMS) (95% CI: -1.1 to 2.38; n = 61). Gabapentin showed no improvement, with a median change of 0 in the treatment group compared to -2 in the placebo group on the SMA Functional Rating Scale (SMAFRS) (n = 66). Hydroxyurea had an MD of -1.88 on the GMFM scale (95% CI: -3.89 to 0.13; n = 57). Phenylbutyrate showed an MD of -0.13 on the Hammersmith Functional Motor Scale (HFMS) (95% CI: -0.84 to 0.58; n = 90). Monotherapy with valproic acid had an MD of 0.06 on the SMAFRS (95% CI: -1.32 to 1.44; n = 31). Very low-certainty evidence suggested that olesoxime and somatotropin had little to no effect on motor function. For olesoxime, the MD was 2 on the Motor Function Measure (MFM) D1 + D2 scale (95% CI: -0.25 to 4.25; n = 160). For somatotropin, the median change at three months was 0.25 points higher on the HFMSE (95% CI: -1 to 2.5; n = 19). A small trial of TRH did not report motor function outcomes, and the certainty of evidence for other outcomes in this trial was low or very low. At the time of this review, results from nine additional trials investigating other treatments, such as 4-aminopyridine, acetyl-L-carnitine, CK-2127107, hydroxyurea, pyridostigmine, riluzole, RO6885247/RG7800, salbutamol, and valproic acid, were not yet available. Ongoing studies are also exploring alternative treatment strategies, including SMN2 augmentation using small molecules. In conclusion, moderate-certainty evidence supports the use of nusinersen for improving motor function in SMA type II. However, creatine, gabapentin, hydroxyurea, phenylbutyrate, valproic acid, and the combination of valproic acid with ALC likely have no clinically meaningful effect on motor function in SMA types II or III. Olesoxime and somatotropin may also have little to no effect, but the evidence is of very low certainty. Further research is needed to evaluate other potential treatments.
